newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda genocide trials in Kigali set to open.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda genocide trials in Kigali set to open.

text.p: Five or six people will be charged on Monday when the first genocide trials in the Rwandan capital open and the government is contemplating possible public executions of those found guilty, senior officials said.
Deputy Justice Minister Gerard Gahima told Reuters: "Five or six people will be put on trial in Kigali starting this morning. We are putting some of the bigger names first."
"We don't know how many people we will be able to get through this week," Gahima said, and named Faoduald Karamira and Silas Munyageshali as two of those to be charged on Monday.
They were expected to enter not guilty pleas.
"If these men are found guilty and sentenced to death, we haven't decided whether executions will be public," he added.

The first genocide trials in Rwanda opened on Friday in the southeastern town of Kibungo, where Deo Bizimana, a former medical assistant, and Egide Gatanazi, a former local administrator, both pleaded not guilty to organising massacres.
Those convicted on charges of taking part in the 1994 slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates face the death penalty after one chance of appeal.

Karamira is a former second vice-president of the Hutu extremist MDR/Power party. Karamira, from the town of Gitarama, was born an ethnic Tutsi but abandoned his roots and was identified and accepted as a Hutu.

He was a senior official of the extremist Interahamwe Hutu militia, accused of playing a leading role in the genocide. Karamira was accused of speaking regularly on the Radio Mille Collines and Rwanda Radio, urging Hutus to slaughter Tutsis.
Munyagashali is a former deputy prosecutor of Kigali.
Gahima did not name other suspects to be charged, but he said another trial would open in the town of Byumba on Tuesday.
There would be no court proceedings in either Kigali or Byumba on New Year's day and the trial would resume on Thursday, Gahima told Reuters.

In Tanzania on Sunday, officials declared an end to an operation to repatriate Rwandan refugees from Tanzania. Aid workers said nearly half a million Rwandan Hutus who fled to Tanzania after the genocide had returned home.
"The operation is winding down, overall it is finished," said Justin Cockerell, a delegate of the International Committee of the Red Cross in the northwestern Tanzanian town of Ngara.

"There no longer appear to be any large refugee groups," he told Reuters by telephone. "We see one or two sporadic family groups. We will be mopping up as clearly some people remain somewhere but it will be nothing like the same scale as before."
